actions.justification: MANDATORY per KDIGO guidelines. This cirrhotic patient has multiple AKI risk factors including hypotension (MAP 66), portal hypertension, ascites, and potential nephrotoxin exposure. Risk factor assessment is the critical first step.

MANDATORY per KDIGO AKI criteria. Oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours) is one of the defining criteria for AKI and is the chief complaint here. Urine output monitoring is essential for staging and tracking progression.

MANDATORY per KDIGO guidelines. Serum creatinine is required to detect AKI, establish current level, and compare against baseline for KDIGO staging (Stage 1: ≥0.3 mg/dL rise or 1.5x baseline; Stage 2: 2x baseline; Stage 3: 3x baseline or ≥4.0 mg/dL).

Critical in cirrhotic patients to differentiate pre-renal AKI from HRS. Patient is hypotensive (MAP 66, BP 88/55) with ascites — volume assessment will guide whether cautious fluid resuscitation is appropriate vs. vasopressor/albumin therapy.

Per KDIGO AKI guidelines, BMP provides BUN, electrolytes, and creatinine trend essential for AKI staging and identifying complications (hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis) in this oliguric cirrhotic patient.

KDIGO guidelines mandate review and discontinuation of nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, diuretics, ACE inhibitors, aminoglycosides) in AKI. Cirrhotic patients on diuretics are particularly vulnerable; discontinuing nephrotoxins is a key early intervention.

KDIGO guidelines recommend urinalysis with microscopy to differentiate pre-renal AKI from intrinsic renal causes (ATN, AIN) and to assess proteinuria. Critical in this cirrhotic patient to distinguish hepatorenal syndrome from other AKI etiologies.

Patient has hypotension (MAP 66, BP 88/55) with ascites/edema — formal hydration assessment is essential to determine if AKI is pre-renal due to effective hypovolemia (common in cirrhosis despite total body fluid overload), guiding fluid management decisions.

Per KDIGO AKI guidelines, nephrotoxic medications (NSAIDs, diuretics, ACE inhibitors, aminoglycosides) must be identified and discontinued. Cirrhotic patients are especially vulnerable; diuretics can precipitate or worsen AKI and should be reviewed.

Establish baseline eGFR to accurately stage AKI severity per KDIGO criteria (creatinine 3.2 suggests Stage 2-3 depending on baseline). Critical for cirrhotic patient to determine extent of renal deterioration and guide nephrology consult threshold.

Urine sodium and FENa are essential to differentiate hepatorenal syndrome (urine Na <10 mEq/L, FENa <1%) from ATN in this cirrhotic patient. This distinction drives management: HRS requires vasoconstrictors (terlipressin/norepinephrine + albumin), while ATN requires supportive care.

CBC needed to evaluate for infection/sepsis (leukocytosis) as precipitant of AKI in cirrhosis (spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is a common trigger), and to assess for anemia and thrombocytopenia common in portal hypertension.
Patient is hemodynamically compromised (MAP 66, BP 88/55, HR 95). Serial vital sign monitoring is essential to track response and detect deterioration in this cirrhotic AKI patient.

FENa calculation is critical to differentiate pre-renal AKI/hepatorenal syndrome (FENa <1%) from intrinsic ATN (FENa >2%) in this cirrhotic patient. This guides fluid and vasopressor management strategy.
With MAP of 66 and BP 88/55, lactate measurement is indicated to assess for tissue hypoperfusion and occult shock, which would impact AKI management and may indicate need for vasopressor support.
Cirrhotic patients with AKI require renal ultrasound to rule out post-renal obstruction (hydronephrosis) as a reversible cause. This is a key step in identifying AKI etiology per KDIGO guidelines.
AKI stage 3 (creatinine 3.2) with oliguria places this patient at high risk for life-threatening hyperkalemia. Active potassium monitoring is critical for patient safety.
Severe AKI can cause metabolic acidosis. Blood gas will assess acid-base status, guide management, and help evaluate need for renal replacement therapy per KDIGO Stage 2-3 guidance.
Comprehensive review of AKI risk factors per KDIGO guidelines including sepsis, nephrotoxin exposure, and hemodynamic instability in this cirrhotic patient to guide targeted management.
Coagulation studies are critical in cirrhosis - coagulopathy is common and affects management decisions including any invasive procedures or paracentesis for worsening ascites.

Patient is hypotensive (MAP 66, BP 88/55) with pre-renal physiology likely contributing to AKI. Cautious crystalloid fluid challenge per KDIGO to optimize renal perfusion, while monitoring closely given ascites and cirrhosis.

Per KDIGO AKI guidelines, nephrotoxic agents (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, contrast) must be discontinued immediately in AKI. This cirrhotic patient with creatinine 3.2 and hypotension is at high risk for further renal injury from nephrotoxins.

Renal ultrasound is indicated to rule out post-renal obstruction as a reversible cause of AKI, and to evaluate renal parenchyma. This is distinct from any prior order and directly follows KDIGO AKI diagnostic workup guidelines.

Urinalysis with microscopy is needed to differentiate pre-renal AKI (hyaline casts, bland sediment) from intrinsic renal disease (muddy brown granular casts suggesting ATN) or infection. Critical for cause identification in this cirrhotic patient.
